Gargi had spent a week writing the annual report for Santosh's logistics firm in Guindy. Twelve pages, charts, a story about their drivers. He replied in four minutes: "Looks ok. Make it more punchy." Nothing else.
The next draft got "Hmm, not sure. Try again." She could see from the shared file that he'd opened it for thirty seconds.
That night, on her balcony, she felt flat and useless. Was she just bad at this?
Then she remembered the two other clients who had praised the same style last month. The problem wasn't her writing. It was that Santosh wasn't really reading.
In the morning she sent three direct questions: "1. Which section feels least punchy? 2. Should the driver story stay, yes or no? 3. Who else needs to approve this?" She added, "A ten-minute call on Thursday would help me finish by Monday."
He replied: "Driver story yes. Call Thursday. My partner decides the rest."

qa.q: How long did Santosh have the second draft open?
qa.a: For thirty seconds, according to the shared file.

qa.a: She felt flat and useless, doubting whether she was simply bad at her work.

Ira's diary, Tuesday night.
A letter from the income tax department came today. I read the first line, "Notice under section...", and my heart started racing. I pictured police. Jail. My parents' faces.
Tejas from the office said, "Don't worry, I know an agent, pay him ten thousand, he'll make it go away." I almost called.
Then I made tea and read the WHOLE notice slowly. It says there's a mismatch between my salary income and what my old employer reported, for last year. It asks me to respond within thirty days. That's it. No police.
Things I did tonight:
- wrote the deadline on my calendar in red
- found my old salary slips and the employer's certificate
- booked an appointment with a chartered accountant Mama recommended, for Saturday
Not calling the agent. Heart still a bit fast. But I know what it says now.

The notice about my property tax came last week. My first reaction was: they're out to get me. Abhinav said, "Just ignore it, they send these to everyone."

passage:
Ujjwal: Devika, I'm at the station. came to report my phone stolen
Ujjwal: the officer wants me to sign a statement. it's in a language I can't read well
Ujjwal: he says just sign, it's routine
Devika: don't sign anything you haven't understood
Ujjwal: he's getting irritated
Devika: stay polite. ask him to read it out to you, or give you a copy
Devika: I'm calling my cousin Rohan, he's a lawyer
Ujjwal: he read it out. it says I "lost" the phone, not that it was stolen
Devika: then ask for it to say stolen. that's what happened
Ujjwal: he said it'll take longer
Devika: that's fine. we'll wait. Rohan says it's your right to have your statement recorded correctly
Ujjwal: ok. he's rewriting it. my hands are shaking lol
Devika: you're doing everything right. not your fault. I'm coming there now
Ujjwal: thank you. getting a copy with the stamp

qa.q: What did the statement say instead of "stolen"?
qa.a: It said Ujjwal had "lost" the phone.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling at the station?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt nervous and pressured, hands shaking, as the officer grew irritated and pushed for a signature.

qa.q: What steps did Devika suggest?
qa.a: Not signing anything unread, asking for it to be read aloud or copied, insisting on the correct word, contacting a lawyer, and getting a stamped copy.

qa.q: How might Devika be feeling while texting?
qa.a: Devika seems worried and protective, calling a lawyer and heading to the station so Ujjwal isn't alone.

grounding: An officer pressures the protagonist to sign an unread statement; they stay calm, refuse to sign blindly, contact a friend and lawyer, and get it recorded correctly.
